problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Element X: from the oxalate to the subchlorides]

2019 is the year of the 150th anniversary of the discovery the Periodic Law by the great Russian scientist D.I. Mendeleev. Dmitri Menedeleev’s genius consists not only in the systematization of all the elements known by that time, but also in the prediction of new elements and their properties. Thus, in 1879, the Swedish chemist Lars Nilson discover a new element $\mathbf{X}$, which is a light silver metal with a characteristic yellowish tinge and related to rare and trace elements. The discovery of $\mathbf{X}$ along with other new elements described by Mendeleev became the triumph of the Periodic Law, showed its predictive power and led to the worldwide recognition of this fundamental law of the universe.

Obtaining of $\mathbf{X}$ is a very difficult task, as it requires enrichment and purification through multiple procedures of extraction and precipitation. In the end, sodium oxalate is added to the enriched solution of $\mathbf{X}$ chloride, resulting in the formation of an insoluble substance $\mathbf{A}$. During the thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ under the temperature less than $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ on air with formation of $\mathbf{B}$ the mass loss is ~ 20%. Upon further heating above $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a white water-insoluble substance $\mathbf{C}$ is formed. The reaction of product $\mathbf{C}$ with sodium fluoride in concentrated hydrochloric acid solution resulting in precipitation of $\mathbf{D}$, that produces chemically pure metal $\mathbf{X}$ under the calcium thermic reaction. Worth noting that complex compound $\mathbf{E}$ is formed due to an excess of sodium fluoride that used for precipitation of $\mathbf{D}$ in industry. Molecular weight of $\mathbf{E}$ 2.235 times higher than that of $\mathbf{D}$.

1. Determine all unknown compound and write the equations of the reactions according to the scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-1-1-fig1.png

Metal $\mathbf{X}$ can form clusters in subhalogenide phases, especially with chlorine, which have become known due to work under supervision of the eminent American scientist J. Corbett. In the $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$ range of subchlorides, the mass fraction of $\mathbf{X}$ increases. $\mathbf{F}$ was synthesized by fusing higher $\mathbf{X}$ metal chloride with powdered $\mathbf{X}$ in a molar ratio of 4:3, respectively, in tantalum crucibles placed in evacuated and sealed quartz ampoules. Prolonged heating of $\mathbf{F}$ leads to its decomposition and the formation of $\mathbf{I}$, the mass loss in this process is 23.95%. The fusion of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is a reaction of coproportionation with the formation of $\mathbf{G}$, during this reaction the oxidation state of $\mathbf{X}$ changes from $\mathbf{F}$ to $\mathbf{G}$ by $\frac{20}{3}\%$ and changes from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{G}$ by 12%. The number of metal atoms in the formula unit of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is the same.

2. Calculate the composition of all subchlorides $\mathbf{F}$ – $\mathbf{I}$ and write the mentioned chemical reaction equations.

Problem 2. [Binary compounds A1–A3 and the salts D1, D2]

The mole fraction of element $\mathbf{X}$ in binary compounds $\mathbf{A1}$, $\mathbf{A2}$ and $\mathbf{A3}$ is 25%, and in compound $\mathbf{A2}$ it is nearly equal to mass fraction. At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ they are solids with ionic crystal structure which decompose at moderate heating. Moreover, at least one simple substance is necessarily present among the decomposition products of each compound. The substance $\mathbf{A3}$ with $\mathbf{X}$ substituted by its lightest analog in the group has a peculiar “mirror twin” $\mathbf{B3}$ (molar fraction of analog of $\mathbf{X}$ equals 75%). The substance $\mathbf{A1}$ can be obtained by the acting of simple substance $\mathbf{Y}$ (gaseous at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) on hydroxide formed by $\mathbf{X}$ at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In this way 1.207 g $\mathbf{A1}$ can be obtained from 1.000 g of hydroxide.

The substances $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$ being in crystalline state contain the same anion as $\mathbf{A1}$, but they possess rather less stability than $\mathbf{A1}$. The substance $\mathbf{D1}$ decompose totally for 48 hours at ambient temperature, and $\mathbf{D2}$ can exist only at temperatures below $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Mass fractions of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen in $\mathbf{D1}$ are equal to 39.33%, 9.90% and 11.47%, respectively, and $\mathbf{D2}$ does not contain carbon. A portion of $\mathbf{D2}$ decompose totally at temperatures above $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, furthermore one of the decomposition products is ionic solid, which can be melt at careful heating (at temperatures above $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) without decomposition, its mass is 1.65 times less than the mass of initial portion.

1. Determine formulas $\mathbf{A1}$, $\mathbf{A2}$, $\mathbf{A3}$ and $\mathbf{B3}$.

2. Write down formulas of three substances which have the same qualitative content as $\mathbf{A1}$, but the different quantitative one.

3. Determine formulas $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$.

4. Write down the molecular equations of the all reactions with $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$, $\mathbf{B3}$, $\mathbf{D2}$ mentioned in the problem.

5. Specify in Answer Sheets the spatial structure of anions in the crystal structures of $\mathbf{A1}$, $\mathbf{A2}$ and $\mathbf{A3}$.

6. Which of binary substances $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A3}$ can be obtained by the direct synthesis starting from simple substances? Write down the equations of respective reactions for their syntheses by such way.

Problem 3. [Cathode and anode materials of lithium-ion batteries]

A cathode of modern lithium-ion batteries contains redox-active lithium salt (for example, lithium iron phosphate) as the active component. This compound can be prepared via heating of an aqueous solution of stoichiometric mixture of $\ce{LiOH}$, $\ce{H3PO4}$, and $\ce{FeSO4}$ at pH 7–8 ($\ce{LiFePO4}$ is the least soluble and is therefore the only reaction product under the said conditions).

1. Write the equation of $\ce{LiFePO4}$ synthesis from the above-listed starting compounds. Determine the stoichiometric ratio between $\ce{LiOH}$ and $\ce{FeSO4}$.

2. Which admixture insoluble phases can be formed along with $\ce{LiFePO4}$ at a) pH < 7 and b) pH > 8?

The following reaction occurs at the cathode during charging of the battery: $\mathrm{LiFePO_4} \rightarrow x\mathrm{Li^+} + x\mathrm{e^-} + \mathrm{Li}_{1-x}\mathrm{FePO_4}$. Specific charge capacity of such cathode is $q_\mathrm{m} = 168\,\mathrm{mA{\cdot}h/g}$, which corresponds to specific energy capacity $E_\mathrm{m} = 580\,\mathrm{W{\cdot}h/kg}$ (in the battery with metal Li as the anode). The Faraday constant is $F = 96500\,\mathrm{Q/mol}$.

3. Write the equation relating the charge capacity of the cathode $q_\mathrm{m}$, molar mass of the formula unit of the active material $M$, and degree of conversion in the cathodic reaction $x$. Determine the degree of conversion of the cathodic reaction involving lithium iron phosphate?

To improve the operational characteristics of the battery, modified cathode materials, for example, $\ce{LiNi_{1/3}Co_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O2}$ are used. For this material, the experimentally determined specific charge capacity equals $160\,\mathrm{mA{\cdot}h/g}$ at average potential of $3.8\,\mathrm{V}$ relative to metal lithium.

4. For the described modified cathode: write the equation of the reaction occurring during charging of the battery and calculate the degree of conversion of the cathodic reaction and specific energy capacity. Basing on the obtained data, select the advantage(s) of this cathode material in comparison with $\ce{LiFePO4}$ (fill in the table in the Answer Sheet).

Graphite or carbon black is usually used as anode of lithium-ion battery. Specific charge capacity of such anode equals $372\,\mathrm{mA{\cdot}h/g}$.

5. Determine the formula of the compound formed during charging of the lithium-ion battery. Write the equation of the occurring reaction.

6. Calculate the total mass of lithium-ion battery (cathode – $\ce{LiNi_{1/3}Co_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O2}$, anode – graphite, mass of other components is 20% of the battery mass) which has the capacity sufficient for charging three times a typical smartphone (its battery capacity is $3500\,\mathrm{mA{\cdot}h}$). Take into account that the highest capacity of the battery is achieved when the ratio of the masses of the cathode and anode equals the ratio between their reciprocal specific capacities.

Problem 4. [Rate-determining steps]

In chemical kinetics a notion “rate-determining step” is often used in study of reaction mechanisms. This notion relates to the approximation in experimental kinetic curves analysis. It is assumed that specific part of the curve or maybe the whole curve corresponds to the particular kinetic step which determines the rate of the complex process under consideration in given moment of time. It was found that in consecutive reactions the slowest step is rate-determining while in parallel reactions the fastest one.

1. For the following scheme of obtaining of the substance $\mathbf{Z}$ (all steps are elementary and take place in solution) find the rate-determining step and prove it via calculation of instantaneous rates, where possible. Consider two cases: (a) $[\mathbf{X}] = 2.0\,\mathrm{M}$, (b) $[\mathbf{X}] = 0.01\,\mathrm{M}$.

$$\begin{array}{ll} 1) & 2\mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z} \quad (k_1 = 6.1\cdot10^{-1}\,\mathrm{M^{-1}min^{-1}}) \\ 2) & \mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y} \quad (k_2 = 8.2\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}) \\ 3) & \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z} \quad (k_3 = 1.0\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M^{-1}min^{-1}}) \end{array}$$

Problem 8. [Back titration of carbon dioxide absorbed by ammonia]

Reverse titration is a technique often used in titrimetry. It involves introducing an excess of titrant and titrating the unreacted titrant upon the completion of the reaction. With that purpose, $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the resulting solution were mixed with $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{BaCl2}$ solution (5 wt.%), $10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.5000\,\mathrm{M}$ NaOH solution, an indicator and an excess of formaldehyde forming hexamethylene tetramine $\ce{(CH2)6N4}$ with ammonia. problems.title: [Moseley's law and X-ray spectra]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Moseley's law and X-ray spectra]

«Periodic law is not threatened with destruction but only superstructures and development are promises …» D.I. Mendeleev

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-1-fig1.png

Figure 1. X-ray spectra

2019 was announced as The International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements and is dedicated to its 150th anniversary. The periodicity of properties is determined by the charge ($Z$) of the atomic nuclei, which was experimentally determined by Henry Moseley in the study of the X-ray spectra of chemical elements. He found that an atom of each chemical element emits X-rays of strictly defined energies. When an electron gets sufficient energy an electron is removed from the inner shell and the atom transitions to an excited state. To return to the ground state, the electron from a further shell must go to the released one. In this case, the excess energy is released in the form of X-rays. The transition from the L-shell to K causes $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$-radiation, the transition M → K gives $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

The wavelength of X-rays emitted during a transition from the energy level $m$ to $n$ is defined as

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(Z-\sigma)^2\left(\frac{1}{n^2}-\frac{1}{m^2}\right),$$

where $R$ – Rydberg constant, $\sigma$ – screening constant, $(Z-\sigma)$ – effective nuclear charge. In general case, the Moseley law can be written as $1/\lambda = C(Z-\sigma)^2$.

1. Determine the constant $C$ (in $R$ units) for $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$- and $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

2. Figure 1 shows a typical view of the X-ray spectrum. Match peaks 1 and 2 with $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$- and $\mathrm{K_\beta}$-radiation.

Figure 2 shows the dependence of $E^{1/2}$ of X-ray $\mathrm{K_\alpha}$-radiation on the atomic number of chemical elements. By the dependence linearization, the equation is obtained $y = a + bx$, where $a = -3.74$; $b = 3.22$.

3. Based on these data and expressions for the Moseley law calculate: a) the screening constant $\sigma$; b) Rydberg constant ($\mathrm{m^{-1}}$).

4. Determine the element $\mathbf{A}$. If you didn’t manage to determine $\sigma$ and $R$ from previous question, accept $R = 3.29\cdot10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\sigma = 1$.

Figure 2. Dependence of X-ray energy on the nuclear charge of elements

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-1-fig2.png

The main sources of X-ray radiation are X-ray tubes and radioisotopes. The voltage ($U$) between the electrodes of the tube determines the minimum wavelength of bremsstrahlung radiation.

5. Determine the voltage (kV) between the electrodes of the X-ray tube that was applied when recording the X-ray spectrum shown in Figure 1. Assume that all the energy $eU$ ($e$ – electron charge) imparted to the electron flux is spent on the generation of X-ray radiation with the energy $h\nu_\mathrm{max}$.

6. a) Calculate the energy that must be given to an atom of the last element ($Z = 30$) from the series shown in Figure 2 for removing an electron from the inner shell.

b) Which of the radioisotopes listed in the table can be used to record the spectra of a number of elements from Figure 2?

Problem 2 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Racemization of a cobalt(III) EDTA complex]

Mellor et al. explained the big difference in the period of the half-life of racemization in the acidic medium of $d$-$\ce{Co(EDTA)^-}$ ($\mathbf{A}$) $\leftrightarrows$ $l$-$\ce{Co(EDTA)^-}$ ($\mathbf{B}$) ($t_{1/2}$ = 2 weeks ($30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and 170 minutes ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)) by the formation of the intermediate $\ce{Co[N2(CH2COO)3CH2COO]^-}$ ($\mathbf{A'}$) with the cleavage of the Co–O bond.

1. Calculate $k_\mathrm{obs}$ ($\mathrm{s^{-1}}$) at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and show that in $r = k_\mathrm{obs}\cdot[\mathbf{A}]$, $[\mathbf{A}]$ and $k_\mathrm{obs}$ depend on pH, considering equilibria $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$); $\mathbf{A'}\mathrm{H} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'} + \ce{H+}$ ($K_\mathrm{a}$) and material balance.

In 1962, Busch et al. denied this mechanism, showing that at pH ≤ 2 $k_\mathrm{obs}$ does not depend on $[\ce{H+}]$ and equals to $4.018\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); $3.110\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). They explained this by trigonal twisting in the intramolecular mechanism (Bailar) $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$); $\mathbf{A'} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ ($k_2$) with the formation of the trigonal prismatic intermediate $\mathbf{A'}$.

2. Calculate $E_\mathrm{a}$ and $\Delta H^{\#}$, $\Delta S^{\#}$, $K^{\#} = k_1/k_{-1}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}$ ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$).

3. Describe the mechanism of $\mathbf{A} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ with structural formulas, derive the kinetic equation using the method of stationary approximations.

In alkaline medium, the racemization rate is much higher and depends on the pH. Thus, at $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $C_\mathbf{A} = 0.01\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, the rate is described by a second-order reaction equation, which is possible in the case of the mechanism: $\mathbf{A} + \ce{OH^-} \leftrightarrows \mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-}$ ($k_3$; $k_{-3}$), $\mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ ($k_4$) with the formation of monocapped trigonal prism $\mathbf{A'}\ce{OH^-}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & 10.30 & 11.50 & 12.26 & 13.02 \\ \hline r,\ \mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s} & 1.08\cdot10^{-6} & 1.71\cdot10^{-5} & 9.83\cdot10^{-5} & 5.65\cdot10^{-4} \end{array}$$

4. Derive the kinetic equation of racemization using the method of stationary approximations, and calculate $k_\mathrm{obs}$ ($\mathrm{L/mol{\cdot}s}$).

5. According to the derived equation, calculate the racemization rate at pH = 5 ($\mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s}$) and compare it with the experimental $8.50\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{mol/L{\cdot}s}$.

As a result, Busch et al came to the conclusion that, at any pH, racemization is described by a two-step mechanism, in which each stage includes two elementary stages, the intermediate is a monocapped trigonal prism, and $k_\mathrm{obs} = k + k' C_{\ce{OH^-}}$

6. Suggest a mechanism common to any pH, derive the kinetic equation.

7. By calculation using this equation, show that the calculated rate for $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the experimental one at pH = 5 coincide.

For reference: $\ln\frac{C^0}{C} = kt$; $k = A\mathrm{e}^{-E_\mathrm{a}/RT}$; $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_\mathrm{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$; $E_\mathrm{a} - \Delta H^{\#} = nRT$; $\Delta S^{\#} = R\left(\ln A - \ln T - \ln\frac{k_\mathrm{B}}{h} - n\right)$, where $n$ – molecularity of the reaction; $t$ – time; $k_\mathrm{B} = 1.381\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$; $h = 6.626\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J{\cdot}s}$.

problems.title: [Transaminases and the King–Altman method]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 2). [Transaminases and the King–Altman method]

Enzymatic reactions involving reversible transfer of an amino group from a donor to an acceptor play the key role in integration of nitrogen and energy metabolism in organisms. Thus, as a result of a transamination reaction, a canonical α-amino acid $\mathbf{A}$ transforms into α-keto acid $\mathbf{B}$ (54.54% O by mass), whereas α-keto acid $\mathbf{C}$ (41.09% C by mass) into canonical α-amino acid $\mathbf{D}$ bearing total negative charge at pH 7. The amino group transfer does not lead to a change of the number of carbon atoms in the donor molecule.

1. Draw structures of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{D}$.

Transamination reactions catalyzed by enzymes referred to as transaminases usually follow the so-called “ping-pong” mechanism, which can be described by the hereunder kinetic scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig1.png

E and E' represent the enzyme in its initial and intermediate states, respectively; $\mathrm{S_1}$ and $\mathrm{S_2}$ are substrates; and $\mathrm{P_1}$ and $\mathrm{P_2}$ are the reaction products.

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the co-factor of transaminases in their initial state. PLP is firmly bound to the protein active site via phosphate group and nitrogen atom making involvement of the latter in the catalysis impossible. It is the amino group of the substrate that interacts with PLP.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig2.png

2. Choose the roles (enzyme, amino group acceptor, amino group donor, enzyme-substrate complex) specific to particles $\mathrm{ES_1}$, $\mathrm{ES_2}$, $\mathrm{S_1}$, and $\mathrm{S_2}$ (scheme (1)).

3. Based on the PLP structure, draw the cofactor forms found in particles $\mathrm{ES_1}$, E', and $\mathrm{E'S_2}$ (scheme (1)).

Kinetics of complicated enzymatic reactions can be described using the King-Altman method based on the graph theory. Let us consider the approach using the two-step Michaelis-Menten scheme as an example:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig3.png

a) First one has to draw a directed graph with the vertices corresponding to all the enzyme forms and the directed edges (arrows) reflecting all possible enzyme transformations. An expression of the reaction rate is attributed to each edge; all such expressions do not include the enzyme in any of its forms (E and ES are not written in the example under consideration).

b) ES transformation into E occurs via two parallel routs: as a result of dissociation ($k_{-1}$) and the product formation ($k_2$). Parallel transformations are summed up ($k_{-1}+k_2$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig4.png

c) Next, one needs to find spanning trees for each vertex of the constructed graph. A tree is defined as a fragment of the initial graph containing all its vertices and a subset of loop-free edges, which allows reaching the target vertex starting from any other one. There is only one spanning tree for each vertex in scheme (2):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-5-fig5.png

d) For each spanning tree, expressions attributed to its edges are multiplied giving the product. If a vertex has several spanning trees, the obtained products are summed up. The finally obtained expression referred to as determinant is denoted as w(En), where En is the vertex under consideration. Thus, for scheme (2) $w(\mathrm{E}) = k_{-1}+k_2$, $w(\mathrm{ES}) = k_1[\mathrm{S}]$.

e) The expression of the reaction rate is given as the determinant of the enzyme form leading to the reaction product multiplied by the rate constant of the step leading to the reaction product and the initial enzyme concentration, divided by the sum of determinants of all the enzyme forms:

$$v = \frac{k_2k_1[\mathrm{S}][\mathrm{E_0}]}{k_{-1}+k_2+k_1[\mathrm{S}]} = \frac{k_2[\mathrm{S}][\mathrm{E_0}]}{K_M+[\mathrm{S}]} \quad \text{where } K_M = \frac{k_{-1}+k_2}{k_1} \qquad (6)$$

4. Draw the directed graph for the “ping-pong” mechanism.

5. Draw all spanning trees for E, $\mathrm{ES_1}$, E', and $\mathrm{E'S_2}$.

6. Write down the determinants $w(\mathrm{E})$, $w(\mathrm{ES_1})$, $w(\mathrm{E'})$, and $w(\mathrm{E'S_2})$.

7. Write down the expression for the rate of $\mathrm{P_2}$ formation.

Problem 10 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 1). [σ- and π-aromaticity]

For most chemists the definition of aromaticity is in the following phrase:

“In order for a molecule to be aromatic, it must contain at least one planar cycle, each of whose atoms has a p-orbital suitable for the formation of an aromatic system. In this cycle there should be 4n+2 (i.e. 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, etc.) electrons”

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-10-fig1.png

Figure 1 German mark dedicated to the discovery of the benzene molecule

Recently, however, the concept of aromaticity has significantly expanded. It was shown that planar systems formed not only by π- but also by σ-bonds can be aromatic, subject to the Hückel’s rule. So, using the expanded definition of aromaticity the following facts can be easily explain:

A. Cation $\mathbf{A}$ with $m/z = 3$ is found in significant quantities in interstellar space

B. Laser evaporation of a mixture of Al with $\ce{Na2CO3}$ leads to formation of a negatively charged $\mathbf{B}$ ion with $m/z = 131$, which has fourth-order symmetry axis.

C. Crystal structure of compound $\ce{Li12Si7}$ is $(\mathrm{Li_6^{6+}}[\mathbf{C}])_2\,(\mathrm{Li_{12}^{10+}}[\mathrm{Si_4}]^{10-})_2$

D. Crystalline sodium amalgam $\ce{Na3Hg2}$ contains square planar anion $\mathbf{D}$.

E. An anion $\mathbf{E}$ was detected during the study of the bimetallic Pt–Zn system in catalytic hydrogenation, the mass spectrum of $\mathbf{E}$ is presented in Fig. 2. It is also known that $\mathbf{E}$ has 5th order symmetry axis and all hydrogen atoms in it are in the same plane with the platinum atom.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-10-fig2.png

Figure 2 Mass-spectra of D anion

In addition to σ-aromatic compounds, chemists managed to obtain molecules, which structures are stabilized with both π-and σ-aromaticity. The history of this type of compounds began in 1988, when it was discovered that oxidation of an orange crystalline binary compound $\mathbf{F}$ (containing 8.65% of element $\mathbf{X}$) in the $\ce{H2O2}$ – $\ce{(CF3SO2)2O}$ – $\ce{CF3SO3H}$ system lead to a blue ionic compound $\mathbf{G}$ (containing 8.49% of element $\mathbf{X}$). The spectral properties of compound $\mathbf{G}$ confirmed its double aromaticity, but it was not possible to investigate its structure in the crystalline state challenged such hypothesis. In the same year, the structure of the purple crystalline ionic compound $\mathbf{N}$ was investigated; however, in this case, it turned out that dication $\mathbf{N}$ was less symmetric than expected. It was possible to unequivocally obtain the compound and prove double aromaticity only in 2018. The synthesis was performed in two stages. In the first stage, the colorless crystalline binary compound $\mathbf{O}$ (containing 13.07% of element $\mathbf{X}$) was treated with an excess of PhSeNa yielding yellow crystals $\mathbf{P}$. Treatment of P with two equivalents of $\ce{NOSbF6}$ led to the formation of green-blue crystals $\mathbf{Q}$ (contains 34.07% of element $\mathbf{X}$). The method is based on the dependence of retention factor $k$, which is calculated using retention times of the retained ($t_\mathrm{r}$) and unretained ($t_\mathrm{m}$) components, on the pH ($\mathrm{pH} = -\lg a_{\mathrm{H^+}}$). The retention factor $k$ for a weak acid is, in its turn, connected with mole fractions of protonated ($\chi_{HA}$) and deprotonated ($\chi_{A^-}$) forms and corresponding retention factors ($k_{HA}$ and $k_{A^-}$):

$$k = \frac{t_\mathrm{r}-t_\mathrm{m}}{t_\mathrm{m}} = \chi_{HA}k_{HA} + \chi_{A^-}k_{A^-}.$$

For diluted aqueous solutions the impact of ionic strength and activity coefficients are usually not considered, but for the investigated buffer–acetonitrile system it can be significant. Therefore, the expression for acid dissociation constant should be written as:

Problem 1. [The acid HX and its derivatives]

Organic derivatives of inorganic acids usually become known much later than the corresponding inorganic salts, but there are some exceptions. Thus, in 1956, Huisgen and Ugi obtained the compound PhX ($\mathbf{A}$), the structure of which was unambiguously proven 27 years later by single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. On the contrary, the studies of the acid HX and its inorganic derivatives were carried out only by quantum chemical methods until the beginning of the 21st century. Thus, in 2001, the existence of the $\ce{FeX2}$ molecule ($\mathbf{B}$) was predicted with the binding energy of the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{2X^-}$ ions forming it only slightly lower than that of the ions in the isoelectronic molecule $\ce{FeY2}$ ($\mathbf{C}$), discovered already in 1951. The light-orange compound $\mathbf{C}$ with the melting point of $173\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the boiling point of $249\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is stable when heated to about $450\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, soluble in organic solvents, including benzene, and insoluble in water. It laid the foundation of a new field of chemistry, which was further included in both inorganic and organic chemistry textbooks.

A derivative of $\mathbf{A}$ was later obtained according to the Huisgen and Ugi procedure from 4-methoxyaniline using NaQ salt. When this new compound was oxidized with ceric(IV) ammonium nitrate (CAN) at $-40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in the presence of zinc nitrate, the formation of a mixed salt $\ce{Zn(X)NO3}$ ($\mathbf{D}$) was observed. When kept at $-20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, this salt decomposes releasing a gas and forming another salt, $\ce{Zn(Q)NO3}$ ($\mathbf{E}$), containing the same elements as $\mathbf{D}$, including 38.59% zinc.

The compound $\mathbf{F}$, an isomer of $\mathbf{B}$, was obtained in 1999. $\mathbf{F}$ is isoelectronic to another known iron compound $\mathbf{G}$, a light-yellow liquid immiscible with cold water. $\mathbf{F}$ dissolves in ethanol, benzene, acetic acid and is used mainly to obtain high-purity iron powder. According to calculations, $\mathbf{F}$ is by $260\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ more stable than $\mathbf{B}$, still the binding energy of the components in it does not exceed $33.7\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$.

In 2017, a stable salt $\mathbf{H}$ was obtained by oxidation of another aryl-X type compound with meta-chloroperbenzoic acid in the presence of iron bis(glycinate). After purification by column chromatography, $\mathbf{H}$ was characterized by single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. It turned out that this salt has a complex composition: it contains X anions, chloride ion, ammonium and hydronium ($\ce{H3O+}$) cations, whereas the content of hydrogen, nitrogen and chlorine in $\mathbf{H}$ is 4.31%, 81.42% and 6.06%, respectively. Starting from this salt, other salts of the acid HX with a variety of cations are obtained by a cation metathesis reaction.

2. Write down equations of the reactions used by Huisgen and Ugi to synthesize PhX.

3. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

The inhabitants of the border regions of the biosphere ought to adapt evolutionarily to extremely strict living conditions. This fact explains that they are usually referred to as extremophiles. In particular, barophiles (for example, some species of fish) are adapted to life under conditions of huge hydrostatic pressure of the ocean depths, which typically causes a disruption in the structure of proteins. In order to minimize the effect of such a press, barophiles produce special low-molecular organic oxygen-containing substances – osmolytes (for example, glycerol or glycine), which stabilize the structure of proteins due to the formation of hydrogen bonds.

The compound $\mathbf{X}$, a major osmolyte in deep-sea organisms, has the carbon to nitrogen mass ratio of 2.57:1. The number of atoms of any of the four elements in the molecule $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as a power of three ($3^m$, where $m$ is an integer).

1. Prove by giving an appropriate mathematical expression (equation) that the molecular weight of any $\mathbf{X}$ with the formula matching the condition given above is always an odd number (provided that $A_r$ are rounded to the nearest integer).

$\mathbf{X}$ is degraded enzymatically according to the reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{X1} + \mathbf{X2}.$$

$\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$ are gaseous substances under standard conditions ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1\,\mathrm{atm}$), toxic to humans. The densities of the substances strictly relate as 3:2, when using the atomic masses of the elements rounded to the nearest integer.

2. Determine the molecular formulas of $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$, keeping in mind that the integrality of the molecular weights is the key idea behind the solution. Show your calculations.

3. Determine the structure of $\mathbf{X}$ if all the carbon atoms in it are equivalent.

Available as a laboratory reagent, white crystalline substance $\mathbf{Y}$ ($M = 111\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), also has osmolyte properties and is used primarily in the study of protein folding to reduce the denaturing effect of urea. $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are identical according to the following: elemental composition (1), mass ratio of carbon and nitrogen (2), equivalence of carbon atoms (3).

4. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Y}$, paying attention to the angles between the bonds.

The compound $\mathbf{Z}$ is another osmolyte in marine organisms. The functioning of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ is due to a similar structural motif. It is known that the number of hydrogen atoms ($N_\mathrm{H} \le 10$) in the molecule of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the product of the numbers (different from each other) of all other atoms (for example, for an arbitrary substance $\mathrm{C}_a\mathrm{H}_b\mathrm{O}_c\mathrm{N}_d$: $b = a \cdot c \cdot d$ with $a \ne c \ne d$).

$\mathbf{Z}$ is degraded enzymatically according to the reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{Z} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z1} + \ce{CH2=CH-COOH}.$$

5. For a theoretical structural formula of $\mathbf{Z}$, devoid of formal intramolecular charges on the atoms, prove by giving the corresponding molecular formula that of the four elements forming it, only one exhibits an odd valence (denote the unknown element $\mathbf{E}$). Indicate which coefficients in the formula support the proof.

$\mathbf{Z1}$ is non-enzymatically oxidized by molecular oxygen dissolved in sea water to a single product, $\mathbf{Z2}$ ($M = 78\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). The molecule of $\mathbf{Z2}$ contains one type of atom of each element.

6. Determine the molecular and structural formulas of $\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{Z1}$ и $\mathbf{Z2}$. Prove by calculations.

problems.problem:
Problem 4. [The glyoxylate cycle]

Metabolism is a paradoxical concept of sustaining life. Although enzymes are incredibly complex in their structure and function, most of substrates, intermediates and products are deceptively simple.

Some species can still grow and develop despite the lack of carbohydrates produced due to photosynthesis or obtained as nutrients. Such organisms can utilize C-2 compounds (molecules containing 2 carbon atoms) as growth substrates. In 1957, Krebs and Kronberg made seminal discovery of a pathway based on glyoxylate (Fig. 1) that solves this problem in plants, prokaryotes, and archaea.

In aqueous solutions, glyoxylic acid exists as a monohydrate (Fig. 2). Spectral analysis suggests an equilibrium with the symmetrical hemiacetal $\mathbf{X}$, formed when the monohydrate reacts with a non-hydrated glyoxylate in a 1:1 molar ratio.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-4-fig2.png

1. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{X}$.

2. Decipher the scheme in Fig. 1 if it is known that all metabolites within the cycle are composed of the same three elements and that the elemental composition in the table refers to the species found under physiological conditions at pH 7.4. Note that all the metabolites are acyclic products, whereas $\mathbf{A4}$ has E-Z isomers.

3. Write down the balanced net equation of the glyoxylate cycle. If needed, show the coenzyme A residue as –SCoA.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Metabolite} & \text{Overall charge (absolute value)} & \omega(\mathrm{C})\ (\%) \\ \hline \mathbf{A1} & 2 & 36.37 \\ \mathbf{A2} & 2 & 36.94 \\ \mathbf{A3} & 3 & 38.11 \\ \mathbf{A4} & 3 & 42.12 \\ \mathbf{A5} & 3 & 38.11 \\ \mathbf{A6} & 2 & 41.39 \end{array}$$

In 1959, Harold Kronberg, Kreb’s student, discovered that glyoxylate is biosynthesized from C-2 precursors $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$.

4. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$, considering the information in the table below.

The following reaction sequence is found in some plants: $\mathbf{X1} \rightarrow \text{glyoxylate} \rightarrow \mathbf{X3}$.

5. From the list (amidase, oxidase, reductase, transamidase), choose the correct enzymes that are responsible for the $\mathbf{X1} \rightarrow \text{glyoxylate}$ and $\text{glyoxylate} \rightarrow \mathbf{X3}$ transformations.

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B1}$, $\mathbf{B2}$, and $\mathbf{B3}$. Note that the last step is catalyzed by aldolase.

7. Propose the scheme of a pathway leading from pyruvate to glyoxylate in organism.

problems.title: [Solubility of nanoparticles and Ostwald ripening]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Solubility of nanoparticles and Ostwald ripening]

The dependence of solubility of a solid substance $c$ on its particle size $r$ obeys the Gibbs–Freundlich–Ostwald equation:

$$c(r) = c_0\, e^{\frac{2\sigma V_\mathrm{m}}{rRT}}$$

($c_0$, $\sigma$, and $V_\mathrm{m}$ are the solubility of the macroscopic phase, specific surface energy, and molar volume of the substance, respectively; $R$ is the universal gas constant; $T$ is the absolute temperature). For a poorly soluble halide $\mathbf{X}$, the solubility of the nanoparticles with $r = 100\,\mathrm{nm}$ is by 9.3% higher compared to the macrophase at the temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\sigma = 450\,\mathrm{mJ/m^2}$, and density $d = 3.18\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

1. Calculate the molar volume of the halide $\mathbf{X}$. If you failed to determine $V_\mathrm{m}$, use $V_\mathrm{m} = 2.95\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^3/mol}$ in further calculations.

2. Calculate the molar mass and determine the formula of the halide $\mathbf{X}$.

The dependence of solubility on the particle size is behind the Ostwald ripening of precipitates. Since the solubility is increased with the decrease in the particle size, a solution saturated with respect to smaller particles is supersaturated with respect to the larger ones. This leads to gradual transfer of the matter from the smaller particles to the larger ones and, hence, overall increase in the particle size of the precipitate.

3. A specimen of the precipitate of $\mathbf{X}$ contains particles with the size of 40, 60, and 80 nm (10 g of each fraction). Calculate the average size of the particles in the specimen. Hereafter consider that the particles are cubic, their size $r$ corresponding to the edge length of the cube.

4. Calculate the solubility of each fraction if the solubility product of the macrophase is $K_\mathrm{sp} = 3\cdot10^{-11}$.

5. Calculate the average particle size in the precipitate once its Ostwald ripening is complete. Consider that ripening is possible if the solubility of the smaller (dissolving) particles exceeds $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, and the difference in the solubilities of the dissolving and growing particles exceeds 5%. Take that the rate of the particles growth is proportional to their initial surface area throughout the entire ripening process.

Problem 6. [The salt X and the gases C and D]

At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the salt $\mathbf{X}$ exists as colorless crystals readily soluble in water. Heating the mixture of $\mathbf{X}$ with either an excess of $\mathbf{A}$ (solid at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $w(\mathrm{O}) = 43\%$ by mass) or an excess of $\mathbf{B}$ (solid at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $w(\mathrm{O}) = 65\%$ by mass) can be used as laboratory methods for obtaining small quantities of gaseous (at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$) binary substances $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$, respectively. $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are readily soluble in water.

If an equimolar amount of $\mathbf{D}$ is introduced into a sealed reactor filled with $\mathbf{C}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$, then the pressure in the reactor decreases to almost zero. The osmotic pressure of the solution prepared from $677\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\mathbf{B}$ and $15.3\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is approximately equal to $1075\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

A saturated (at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) aqueous solution of $\mathbf{D}$ remains practically colorless when stored in air. To determine the concentration of $\mathbf{D}$ in such a solution, an aliquot of $1.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ was titrated with a pre-standardized $\ce{NaOH}$ solution. $26.13\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the alkali solution was consumed. To standardize the alkali solution, the hydrochloric acid was prepared as follows. A $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the $\ce{HCl}$ solution saturated at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (41.8% by mass, density $1.202\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) was placed in a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and brought to the mark with water. $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the prepared hydrochloric acid was consumed to standardize a $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the alkali solution.

1. Determine the composition and give the formulas of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{X}$. Support by calculations.

2. Write the equations of all the reactions described.

problems.title: [Intermolecular interactions]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Intermolecular interactions]

Interactions between molecules, atoms and ions are referred to as intermolecular. These are much weaker than the forces of covalent and ionic interactions, but their play a very important role. The energy ($E_1$) of the interaction of two atoms at the distance between the centers of which equals $R$ can be calculated using the equation:

$$E_1 = b\exp(-aR) - \frac{d}{R^6}.$$

The first term in this equation is responsible for repulsion which leads to an increase in the energy of the system, whereas the second one is responsible for the attraction between instantly induced dipoles which leads to a decrease in the energy of the system. Repulsion predominates at short distances, while attraction prevails at larger ones. Constants $a$, $b$ and $d$ depend on the electronic structure of the particles. The values of these constants (in atomic units, a.u.) for some pairs of atoms obtained from experimental data are given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{He–He} & \text{He–Ne} & \text{He–Ar} & \text{He–Kr} & \text{He–Xe} \\ \hline a & 2.10 & 2.27 & 2.01 & 1.85 & 1.83 \\ b & 6.55 & 33.0 & 47.9 & 26.1 & 42.4 \\ d & 2.39 & 4.65 & 15.5 & 21.85 & 33.95 \end{array}$$

When doing calculations, you should use the value of $R$ in atomic units (a.u.). Potential energy is also obtained in a.u. A negative value of $E_1$ means that the energy of the system at this distance is by the value equal to the absolute value of $E_1$ less than the energy at an infinite distance between particles.

1. Calculate $E_1$ for the system of two He atoms for the distances $R$ equal to 5.00 a.u. and 7.00 a.u.

2. Using the method of successive approximations, estimate the maximum value by which the energy of the system of two He atoms can decrease due to intermolecular interaction.

If the interacting particles are charged, then the Coulomb interaction additionally arises between them, the potential energy of which ($E_2$, in a.u.) can be calculated using the formula:

$$E_2 = \frac{q_1 q_2}{R},$$

where $q_1$ and $q_2$ are the charges of particles in a.u. (1 a.u. of charge is equal to the absolute value of the electron charge), $R$ is the distance in a.u.

3. Let us consider the LiF molecule with a 100% ionic bond. The distance between the centers of the nuclei is $152\,\mathrm{pm}$. Calculate the energy of dissociation of the LiF molecule into ions:

$$\ce{LiF(g) = Li^+(g) + F^-(g)}.$$

Note: Isoelectronic particles have the same constants in the equation for $E_1$.

(If you failed to calculate the dissociation energy of LiF, then take it as $20.0\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$ in further calculations).

4. The ionization energy of the lithium atom is $5.39\,\mathrm{eV}$, and the electron affinity energy of the fluorine atom is $3.45\,\mathrm{eV}$. Calculate the molar bond energy of LiF.

Additional reference materials: 1 a.u. of length = $52.9\,\mathrm{pm}$; 1 a.u. of energy = $27.21\,\mathrm{eV}$.

problems.title: [Rotational-vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical chemistry section, problem 1). [Rotational-vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules]

Diatomic are the simplest molecules. Accordingly, they have been investigated in detail both theoretically and experimentally. Rotational-vibrational spectroscopy is among the most important methods for studying diatomic molecules. The “Harmonic oscillator – rigid rotator” approximation is a basic model for the description of the vibrational-rotational spectra. Within this model, the types of intermolecular motion under discussion are independent, whereas their energy levels are as follows:

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \omega_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right), \qquad E_\mathrm{rot} = B_e J(J+1),$$

where $\omega_e = h\nu$ is the vibrational constant, $\nu$ is the frequency of vibrations, $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ is the vibrational quantum number, $B_e = h^2/(8\pi^2\mu r_e^2)$ is the rotational constant, $\mu = m_\mathrm{A}m_\mathrm{B}/(m_\mathrm{A} + m_\mathrm{B})$ is the reduced mass of the molecule, $r_e$ is the equilibrium internuclear distance, $J = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ is the rotational quantum number. Only $(n, J) \rightarrow (n \pm 1, J \pm 1)$ transitions are allowed.

For the HF molecule, the energy of transition from the ground vibrational, ground rotational level to the first vibrational, first rotational level equals $\Delta E(0, 0 \rightarrow 1, 1) = 4180.23\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; the energy of transition from the ground vibrational, first rotational level to the first vibrational, ground rotational level is $\Delta E(0, 1 \rightarrow 1, 0) = 4096.41\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

1. Calculate $\omega_e$ and $B_e$ in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

2. Calculate $\nu$ in Hz and $r_e$ in Å.

The model of anharmonic oscillator allows a more precise description of the molecular vibrations. In this model, the energy of the $n$th vibrational level equals:

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \omega_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right) - \omega_e x_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2,$$

where $\omega_e x_e$ is the anharmonicity constant. Decrease in the distance between the neighboring levels ($n$ and $n + 1$) is a specific feature of the model. This leads to the equality of energies $E_\mathrm{vib}(n)$ and $E_\mathrm{vib}(n + 1)$ for a definite $n_\mathrm{max}$, which is due to the absence of the vibrational levels for $n > n_\mathrm{max}$, since the molecule dissociates into atoms above this level.

3. Express $n_\mathrm{max}$ in terms of $\omega_e$ and $\omega_e x_e$.

4. Express the dissociation energy in terms of $\omega_e$ and $\omega_e x_e$.

Beside this, the rotational-vibrational interaction can occur, due to which the rotational constant $B_e$ depends on vibrational state $n$:

$$E_\mathrm{rot} = B_n J(J+1), \qquad B_n = B_e - \alpha_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right),$$

where $\alpha_e$ is the constant of the rotational-vibrational interaction.

5. From the following options, select those, which correctly explain why $B_n$ depends on $n$:
the kinetic energy of rotation of the molecule increases with an increase of $n$;
the average bond length in the molecule changes with an increase of $n$;
due to the repulsion of the atoms, the molecule is rather stretched than compressed during oscillations;
due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the bond length permanently changes.

Methylidyne CH is the smallest molecule, which can be notionally named organic. Though the radical its extremely unstable, it was detected spectroscopically in the so-called CH-stars. Also, it is involved in the Fischer–Tropsch process. Spectral properties of CH are well studied. The energies ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of some rotational-vibrational transitions are given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & n = 0 \rightarrow n = 1 & n = 1 \rightarrow n = 2 \\ \hline J = 0 \rightarrow J = 1 & 2759.77 & 2632.66 \\ J = 1 \rightarrow J = 2 & 2785.97 & 2657.79 \end{array}$$

6. Using the data in the table, calculate $\omega_e$, $\omega_e x_e$, $B_e$, and $\alpha_e$ in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

7. Using the expression derived in i. 4, calculate the dissociation energy of the C−H bond in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. If you failed to answer i. 4, use the approximate formula $E \approx \omega_e^2/(4\omega_e x_e)$.

8. Calculate the length of the C−H bond in Å.

Reference materials:

Masses of isotopes (a.m.u.): $m(\mathrm{F}) = 18.9984$, $m(\mathrm{C}) = 12.0000$, $m(\mathrm{H}) = 1.0078$.

Conversion of reciprocal centimeters to joules: $E(\mathrm{J}) = 100hcE(\mathrm{cm^{-1}})$.

$h = 6.626\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$ is the Planck constant, $c = 2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is the speed of light, $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ is the Avogadro’s number.

problems.title: [Ligand field theory and magnetic susceptibility]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Physical chemistry section, problem 2). [Ligand field theory and magnetic susceptibility]

Despite its simplicity, the Ligand Field Theory (LFT) satisfactorily explains most of the magnetic and spectral properties of complex compounds of transition elements. Ligands are considered as a source of an electrostatic field with certain symmetry, acting on the electronic system of the central ion. The field shifts the energy levels (terms) of the free ion and splits them. The magnitude and nature of splitting depend on the field strength of the ligands and their location.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig1.png

Figure 1

Fig. 1 shows the shape of the five $d$-orbitals of a free atom or ion and the arrangement of ligands in an octahedral environment. The three orbitals in the top row are geometrically equivalent. The two orbitals in the bottom row are also equivalent to each other, despite their different appearance.

1. What is the degeneracy factor ($g$) of the energy level of a free ion with a single $d$-electron over the closed shells?

2. Draw a diagram of the level splitting of the central ion in the octahedral complex $\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^{3+}}$. For split levels, give Mulliken notation based on the symbols for irreducible representations of group theory.

In an octahedral field, the levels are split in the proportion 3 : 2 (relative to the “center of gravity”, i.e. the energy of an ion placed in a spherical shell with the charge equal to the sum of the ligand charges). Let us denote the energy interval between split levels as $\Delta_o$, and the pairing energy of electrons in one orbital as $P$.

3. Distribute electrons onto the energy levels for the low-spin (LS) and high-spin (HS) the states of the complex with the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion. Indicate the total spin $S$ of the complex and the type of magnetism (paramagnetic/diamagnetic).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig2.png

4. Find the relationship between $\Delta_o$ and $P$, at which the energies of the LS and HS states of the octahedral complex formed by the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion are the same.

For the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion $P = 17600\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and for the complexes $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}}$ $\Delta_o = 10400\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $33000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, respectively.

5. Which one is high-spin and which one is low-spin?

Fig. 2 shows the dependence of the term energy of the $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ ion in an octahedral field on the strength of the ligands. For $\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]^{2+}}$ $\Delta_o = 10800\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig3.png

Figure 2

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig4.png

Figure 3

6. How many bands are there in the absorption spectrum associated with the $d$–$d$ transitions from the ground electronic state of this complex (choose the correct answer: 3, 6 or 9)? Predict the frequencies ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of the absorption band maxima.

The magnetic susceptibility of a unit volume of a substance $\chi_\mathrm{V}$ (a dimensionless quantity) can be measured by the Gouy method following the apparent change in the mass of the sample in a non-uniform magnetic field (Fig. 3). The magnetic force acting on the sample is:

$$F = \tfrac{1}{2}\chi_\mathrm{V} H^2 \sigma\ \mathrm{dyn}, \qquad (1)$$

where $H$ is the field strength (Gauss, Gs) at the level of the ampoule bottom, $\sigma$ is the ampoule cross section area ($\mathrm{cm^2}$).

The empiric formula for calculating the specific susceptibility (per 1 g of substance) of Mohr’s salt $\ce{(NH4)2Fe(SO4)2*6H2O}$ is:

$$\chi_\mathrm{S} = \frac{9.5}{T+1}\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^3/g}, \qquad (2)$$

where $T$ is the temperature in Kelvins. The salt crystals have a cubic structure with the lattice parameter $a = 1.2318\,\mathrm{nm}$, the unit cell contains $Z = 4$ formula units. The salt is placed in a cylindrical ampoule with the diameter $d = 1.4\,\mathrm{cm}$. At $H = 5000\,\mathrm{Gs}$, $\Delta m = 0.868\,\mathrm{g}$.

7. Determine the density $\rho$ ($\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) of the Mohr’s salt crystals and calculate $\chi_\mathrm{S}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming that the sample is tightly packed in the ampoule, calculate the $\chi_\mathrm{V}$ of Mohr’s salt.

On the other hand, the molar susceptibility can be expressed as

$$\chi_\mathrm{M} = \frac{N_\mathrm{A}\mu_\mathrm{eff}^2}{3k_\mathrm{B}T}\ \mathrm{cm^3\cdot mol^{-1}}, \qquad (3)$$

where $N_\mathrm{A}$ is the Avogadro’s number, $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant, $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective magnetic moment of the central ion in Bohr magnetons $\mu_\mathrm{B} = 0.917\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm{erg/Gs}$.

8. Find $\chi_\mathrm{M}$ and determine $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ of Mohr’s salt in Bohr magnetons at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Expression (3) does not account for the constantly present diamagnetism reducing the susceptibility. The magnetic moment, which is due only to the spin of the central ion, is given as (in Bohr magnetons):

$$\mu_S = 2\sqrt{S(S+1)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}, \qquad (4)$$

where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

9. Assuming that the magnetic moment of Mohr's salt is determined only by the spin of the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion, use the expression (4) to estimate whether this complex is low-spin or high-spin.

Reference materials:

Problem 6 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 3). [Blood alcohol content]

Alcohol, depending on its content in the human body, leads to various negative effects. Blood alcohol content (BAC) is usually calculated as the mass of ethanol (g) in a unit volume of blood (L) or expressed as a percentage (BAC of 1% corresponds to 1 g of ethanol in 100 mL of blood). The Widmark formula can be used to estimate BAC (in g/L) from the amount of alcohol consumed:

$$\mathrm{BAC} = \frac{a}{V_\mathrm{d}} - \beta t = \frac{a}{m\cdot k_\mathrm{d}} - \beta t,$$

where $a$ is the mass of ethanol consumed (g); $V_\mathrm{d}$ is the volume of ethanol distribution in the body (L); $m$ is the mass of a person (kg); $k_\mathrm{d}$ is the Widmark distribution coefficient, which is equal to 0.71 and $0.58\,\mathrm{L/kg}$ for males and females, respectively; $\beta$ is the rate of ethanol elimination, averaging $0.15\,\mathrm{g/(L\cdot h)}$; $t$ is the time since alcohol consumption (h).

1. Calculate how many times the lethal dose of ethanol for a female weighing 60 kg is less than that for a male weighing 80 kg. Consider that the effect of alcohol is determined only by its concentration in the blood, regardless of gender.

The vast majority of countries have BAC limits for drivers. The maximum allowed BAC ranges from 0 (total ban) to 0.08%, e.g. in China the BAC limit is 0.02%.

2. Calculate the maximum volume $V_\mathrm{max}$ (mL) of the Chinese alcoholic beverage Huangjiu ("yellow wine") with the ethanol content ($\varphi$) of 10 vol.% that can be drunk by a male weighing 80 kg 30 min before driving. The density of pure ethanol ($\rho$) is $0.789\,\mathrm{g/mL}$.

Note! Despite acceptable BAC values other than 0 (which is due to metabolic peculiarities in different people), drinking alcohol before driving is extremely unsafe!

The determination of BAC can be carried out using a variety of analytical methods. For quick analysis, such as when checking drivers on the road, breathalyzers are used to determine the amount of ethanol in one’s breath. One of the first breathalyzers was developed by R.F. Borkenstein. Exhaled air was passed through a solution of $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ in the presence of $\ce{H2SO4}$ and small amounts of $\ce{AgNO3}$. The intensity of the color change from orange to blue-green was used to conclude the degree of intoxication of the person being tested.

3. Write down the reaction equation that underlies the Borkenstein breathalyzer.

To find the amount of reacted $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ and thus ethanol in the sample, it is possible to use the spectrophotometric method. The table summarizes the results of absorbance ($A$) measurements from testing people with different levels of BAC. Measurements were made at a wavelength at which absorbance by the reaction products can be neglected. The volume of solution in the breathalyzer is 3.0 mL and the volume of exhaled air is 1.0 L. Assume that 1 mL of blood contains on average the same amount of ethanol as 2100 mL of exhaled air.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{BAC} & 0.000\% & 0.030\% & 0.060\% & 0.100\% & 0.150\% \\ \hline A & 0.898 & 0.640 & 0.382 & 0.150 & 0.150 \end{array}$$

4. Calculate the maximum $\mathrm{BAC_{max}}$ value (%) that can be numerically determined with this breathalyzer.

5. Calculate the concentration $c(\ce{K2Cr2O7})_0$ (mM) in the stock solution. Assume that the volume of the solution in the breathalyzer does not change when passing the analyzed breath.

In hospitals, an enzymatic assay (EA) is often used to determine BAC. For this, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is added to blood serum, resulting in the oxidation of ethanol with the coenzyme $\ce{NAD+}$. The BAC can be calculated by measuring the absorbance of the solution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-6-fig1.png

6. Write down the equation of the reaction occurring during the EA of ethanol in blood serum.

7. Using the given UV absorption spectrum of $\ce{NAD+}$ and NADH, give the value of wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) that is optimal for measuring the absorbance for BAC calculation.

When analyzing samples with a complex matrix, such as blood serum, the method of standard additions is used. For this purpose, known amounts of the determined substance are introduced into the analyzed sample, and the EA of the resulting solutions is carried out. As a result of such analysis, the following calibration dependence of absorbance ($A$) on the concentration of added ethanol ($c_\mathrm{add}$, $\mathrm{\mu M}$) was obtained: $A = 6.20\cdot10^{-3}\cdot c_\mathrm{add} + 0.155$. Calibration solutions were prepared by adding the calculated amounts of the standard ethanol solution to the $100\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ aliquots of blood serum followed by dilution with the physiological solution to 1.00 mL.

This dependence of $T_\mathrm{c}$ on the molar mass of an isotope is referred to as the isotopic effect; for many superconductors the dependence can be written as $T_\mathrm{c} \sim \mathrm{const}/M^\zeta$. Problem 12 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 3). [Hydrogen cations, hydride anions and dihydrogen complexes]

For a long time, hydrogen was believed to form the $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ ions in gaseous phase, and the $\ce{H2+}$ particle under gas discharge at low pressure. Later, the molecular cation $\ce{H3+}$ was discovered in gas discharges (Thomson) and in the atmosphere of hydrogen planets (Mac Nab). Relatively recently, it was shown that the $\ce{H2}$ molecules can attach to $\ce{H3+}$ to form $\ce{H5+}$, $\ce{H7+}$, and $\ce{H9+}$.

1. Draw the structure of the $\ce{H3+}$ cation, if the hydrogen atoms are equidistant from each other. Draw the overlap of the $s$-orbitals of the atoms and choose what type of bond is formed in the $\ce{H3+}$ cation. Draw the structures of the cations $\ce{H5+}$, $\ce{H7+}$ and $\ce{H9+}$, in which 3 atoms form right triangle in the mirror symmetry plane, while other atoms are in the planes perpendicular to the latter and containing the medians of the triangle.

In an aqueous solution, the existence of bound $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ as parts of compounds is possible.

2. Write the reactions that describe the behavior of unbound $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ in an aqueous solution. By calculating $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ of the reaction $\ce{H2O + H- -> }\ldots$ ($E^\circ_{\ce{H2/H-}} = -2.23\,\mathrm{V}$; $E^\circ_{\ce{H2O/H2}} = -0.83\,\mathrm{V}$) prove that the existence of an unbound $\ce{H-}$ in the solution is impossible.

The $\ce{H-}$ anion, which is unstable in solution, is stabilized in complexes with the formation of a M−H bond. Like $\ce{H+}$, it most often has the CN = 1. At the same time, it turned out that in hydrides $\ce{H-}$ can form bridges and have the CN up to 6.

3. Draw the structures of $\mathrm{HM}_n$ fragments in the complexes: $\ce{[(CO)5WHW(CO)5]+}$ (angle MHM < 180°); $\ce{[HRh3(C5H5)4]}$ (angle close to 109.5°); $\ce{[HCo6(CO)15]-}$ (angles of 90 and 180°).

Hydrides are often obtained by an oxidative addition reaction, which occurs with the oxidation of the M complex: cis-$\ce{[MClCO(PPh3)2]} + n\ce{H2} = \mathbf{A}$, Ph = $\ce{C6H5}$. In the mechanism of oxidative addition, an intermediate formation precedes that of the hydride $\mathbf{A}$. This is accompanied by the appearance of the band $\nu \sim 1500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectrum of the hydride $\mathbf{A}$ (in $\ce{H2}$ $\nu = 4160\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), whereas the $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distance changes from 0.074 nm in $\ce{H2}$ to ~0.170 nm in the hydride.

4. Decipher M, if $\omega_\mathrm{Cl} = 4.53\%$, and $\omega_\mathrm{H} = 4.13\%$ in $\mathbf{A}$. Give the formula of $\mathbf{A}$, the number of electrons around M, and the oxidation state of M in the original complex and in $\mathbf{A}$. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

The researchers failed to synthesize the intermediate of the oxidative addition reaction until 1980, when Kubas managed to stop the reaction at the step of the intermediate formation. After passing hydrogen ($p = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$) for 20 min through a dark purple solution in toluene containing 4.1442 g of trans-$\ce{[M'(CO)3(PCy3)2]}$, Cy = $\ce{C6H11}$, he isolated 3.74 g of the yellow crystals $\mathbf{B}$ containing the ligand L (the reaction yield was of about 90%). The band appears at $\nu = 2690\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectrum of the complex $\mathbf{B}$; the bond length $r_\mathrm{H-H} = 0.084\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $\omega_\mathrm{M'} = 22.13\%$ in $\mathbf{B}$.

5. Decipher M’ and $\mathbf{B}$. Draw its spatial structure.

It is rarely possible to stop the reaction at the intermediate step. Even if it looks like so, a mixture of the intermediate and hydride is usually formed, because their thermodynamic characteristics are close. Thus, Luo and Harbtree obtained a product as a result of the treatment of $\ce{[ReCl3(CO)(PMe2Ph)3]}$ with $\ce{LiAlH4}$ in ether at 193.2 K. Addition of $\ce{HBF4*OEt2}$ in $\ce{CD2Cl2}$ at 193.2 K to the product leads to an equilibrium mixture of $\mathbf{D}^+$ and $\mathbf{E}^+$ cations. For equilibrium $\mathbf{D}^+ \rightleftarrows \mathbf{E}^+$, the enthalpy $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ is $-4.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, and the entropy $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ$ is $-10\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$.

6. Determine the formulas of $\mathbf{D}^+$ and $\mathbf{E}^+$, if there are two $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distances (0.087 and 0.180 nm) in the structure of $\mathbf{E}^+$ and only one $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distance (0.176 nm) in that of $\mathbf{D}^+$.

7. Calculate the equilibrium constant and the composition of the equilibrium mixture $\chi$ in mol%.

Analysis of the synthesized compounds showed that different ligands in the complex can contribute to the formation of either the intermediate or hydride.

8. Give the MO diagram for the ligand L and calculate the bond multiplicity in it. Indicate with an arrow the possible direction of the electron transfer between $\pi_d$-orbitals of M and molecular orbitals of L.

Problem 2. [Wöhler’s compound]

The beginning of organic chemistry as a science can be dated to 1828, when Friedrich Wöhler first synthesized the organic compound $\mathbf{A}$ (20.00 wt% carbon, 46.65 wt% nitrogen, and 26.64 wt% oxygen) under laboratory conditions. Remarkably, it was obtained from an inorganic substance that is an isomer of $\mathbf{A}$. Today, $\mathbf{A}$ is a multi-ton industrial product, widely used in agriculture as the mineral fertilizer richest in nitrogen.

I-2.1 (0.5 pt) Provide the structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

I-2.2 (0.5 pt) Provide the structure of the compound from which $\mathbf{A}$ was first synthesized.

I-2.3 (0.5 pt) $\mathbf{A}$ is currently produced on industrial scale via a two-step process. Provide the chemical equations of the reactions involved.
